title: What Are Passwords and How Does Hashing Work?

scenes.narration: Every time you log in to a website, you trust it to handle your password safely. But what happens if someone breaks into that website's database? The answer depends partly on how the website stores your password. In this video, we'll explore password hashing, see how it works, and learn how developers protect login systems.

Imagine a website storing every password as plain text. If a database leak exposes those records, attackers can read them directly. The damage can spread when people reuse the same password on other websites. Secure systems should never need to keep your original password in a readable form just to verify your next login.

visual.title: The danger of plain text
items: Passwords stored as plain text
A database leak exposes records
Attackers read them directly
People reuse the same password

scenes.narration: A hash function takes input and produces a fixed-length output. The same input produces the same result for the same hash settings, while different inputs will usually produce different results. A properly designed cryptographic hash is intended to be one-way: you cannot simply reverse the output to recover the original password. But ordinary fast hashes alone are not enough for secure password storage.

visual.title: How hashing works
items: Input becomes a fixed-length output
The same input gives the same result
Different inputs usually give different results
You cannot simply reverse the output

scenes.narration: Here is a simplified JavaScript example using the Argon2 library in a server environment. First, the application receives a password. The library creates a password hash with a salt and the required settings. The output is what the application stores in its database, rather than the original password. This is illustrative code; it requires the appropriate library and server-side setup.

visual.title: Hash a password with Argon2
visual.code: const storedHash = await argon2.hash(password);\n\nawait argon2.verify(storedHash, candidatePassword);
visual.output: Store the encoded hash, not the password

scenes.narration: What happens when you return and log in? The server receives the candidate password you entered and uses the password-hashing library to check it against the stored hash. The library uses the salt and parameters recorded with that hash. It does not decrypt the stored hash. If the check succeeds, access is granted; if it fails, the application rejects the login.

visual.title: Checking a login
items: The library does not decrypt the hash
It checks the candidate password
It uses the stored hash and its settings
Access is granted only after a match

scenes.narration: Secure password storage needs more than a basic hash. A unique salt helps ensure that identical passwords do not produce identical stored values. Password-hashing algorithms are deliberately slow by design, making large-scale guessing more expensive. Developers commonly choose Argon2id or bcrypt, depending on their system and requirements. They should never use SHA-256 alone as their password-storage method.

visual.title: Better password storage
items: Give each password a unique salt
Use hashing that is slow by design
Choose Argon2id or bcrypt appropriately
Never use SHA-256 alone for passwords

scenes.narration: Hashing is important, but it is only one layer of security. Encourage users to create long unique passwords and keep them in a trusted password manager. Add multi-factor authentication where possible. On the server, apply rate limits, monitor suspicious login attempts, protect secrets, and keep software updated. Security comes from several layers working together, not from one clever function.

visual.title: Protect real accounts
items: Use long unique passwords
Use a trusted password manager
Enable multi-factor authentication
Apply rate limits to login attempts

scenes.narration: Let's recap. Password hashing helps websites verify passwords without storing the original text. Salts and dedicated password-hashing algorithms make stolen password databases harder to attack, although no method guarantees perfect security. If you are learning backend development, understanding this process is an essential step toward building safer applications. Subscribe to Concept in Motion for more technology explained simply.
